title: No. 52 — The House of Representatives (Madison)
paragraphs: The first thing to examine in this part of the government is the qualifications of the electors and of the elected. The electors are to have the same qualifications as those who elect the most numerous branch of the State legislatures. The definition of the right of suffrage is very justly regarded as a fundamental article of republican government, so the Convention was bound to define and establish this right in the Constitution. To leave it open to occasional regulation by Congress would have been improper, for the reason just given. To leave it to the legislative discretion of the States would have been improper for the same reason. It would also have made too dependent on the State governments a branch of the federal government that ought to depend on the people alone. To reduce the different qualifications in the different States to one uniform rule would probably have displeased some of the States as much as it would have been difficult for the Convention. The provision the Convention made therefore appears to be the best of the choices open to it. It must satisfy every State, because it conforms to the standard that the State itself has already established, or may establish. It will be safe for the United States because, being fixed by the State constitutions, it cannot be altered by the State governments; and there is no reason to fear that the people of the States will alter this part of their constitutions so as to cut down the rights the federal Constitution secures to them.

The State constitutions define the qualifications of the elected less carefully and properly, and these qualifications are also better suited to uniformity. The Convention has therefore very properly considered and regulated them itself. A representative of the United States must be twenty-five years old, must have been a citizen of the United States for seven years, must be an inhabitant of the State he is to represent at the time of his election, and must hold no office under the United States while he serves. Under these reasonable limits, the door to this part of the federal government stands open to merit of every description, whether native or adoptive, young or old, poor or rich, and without regard to any particular profession of religious faith.

The term for which the representatives are to be elected comes under a second view of this branch. To decide whether this article is proper, two questions must be considered: first, whether biennial elections will be safe in this case; secondly, whether they are necessary or useful.

First. Liberty requires that the government in general have a common interest with the people, and it requires in particular that the branch we are considering depend directly on the people and feel close sympathy with them. Frequent elections are without question the only policy that can effectively secure this dependence and sympathy. But how frequent they must be to do it cannot, it seems, be calculated exactly, and depends on a variety of circumstances connected with the matter. Let us consult experience, the guide that ought always to be followed whenever it can be found.

Ancient forms of government knew the scheme of representation, as a substitute for a meeting of the citizens in person, only very imperfectly at best. We should therefore expect instructive examples only from more modern times. Even among these, to avoid a search too vague and sprawling, we should limit ourselves to the few examples that are best known and most closely resemble our own case. The first one that fits this description is the House of Commons in Great Britain. The history of this branch of the English Constitution before Magna Charta is too obscure to teach anything. Students of political antiquities have even questioned whether it existed. The earliest records from after that date show only that parliaments were to SIT every year, not that they were to be ELECTED every year. Even these annual sessions were left so much to the monarch's discretion that royal ambition, under various pretexts, often arranged very long and dangerous gaps between them. To remedy this grievance, a statute in the reign of Charles II provided that the gaps should not be stretched beyond three years. When William III came to the throne and a revolution took place in the government, the subject was taken up again, more seriously, and it was declared to be among the fundamental rights of the people that parliaments ought to be held FREQUENTLY. Another statute, passed a few years later in the same reign, gave the word "frequently," which had referred to the three-year period fixed under Charles II, a precise meaning: it expressly enacted that a new parliament must be called within three years after the end of the previous one. The last change, from three years to seven, is well known to have come fairly early in the present century, under an alarm for the Hanoverian succession. These facts show that the greatest frequency of elections ever thought necessary in that kingdom to bind the representatives to their constituents is no more than a return every three years. And if we may argue from the degree of liberty that survives even under septennial elections and all the other vicious ingredients in the parliamentary constitution, we cannot doubt that cutting the period from seven years to three, together with the other needed reforms, would extend the people's influence over their representatives enough to satisfy us that biennial elections under the federal system cannot possibly endanger the dependence the House of Representatives must have on its constituents.

Until recently, the crown regulated elections in Ireland entirely at its own discretion. They were seldom repeated except when a new prince acceded or some other chance event occurred. The parliament that began with George II lasted through his whole reign, about thirty-five years. The representatives depended on the people only in that the people could fill occasional vacancies by electing new members, and in the chance of some event that might bring on a general new election. The Irish parliament's ability to defend the rights of its constituents, so far as it was inclined to, was also badly shackled by the crown's control over the subjects it could deliberate on. Lately, if I am not mistaken, these shackles have been broken, and octennial parliaments have also been established. What effect this partial reform will have must be left to further experience. Seen in this light, then, the example of Ireland can throw little light on the subject. If any conclusion can be drawn from it, it can only be this: if the people of that country have managed, under all these disadvantages, to keep any liberty at all, then biennial elections would give them every degree of liberty that depends on a proper connection between their representatives and themselves.

Let us bring our inquiries closer to home. The example of these States when they were British colonies deserves particular attention, though it is so well known that little needs to be said about it. All of them had established the principle of representation, in one branch of the legislature at least. But the periods of election differed, varying from one year to seven. Do we have any reason to infer, from the spirit and conduct of the representatives of the people before the Revolution, that biennial elections would have endangered the public liberties? The spirit that appeared everywhere at the start of the struggle, and that overcame the obstacles to independence, is the best proof that a sufficient measure of liberty had been enjoyed everywhere to inspire both a sense of its worth and a zeal for properly enlarging it. This holds as true for the colonies with the least frequent elections as for those with the most frequent. Virginia was the colony that took the lead in resisting the parliamentary usurpations of Great Britain, and the first to adopt, by public act, the resolution of independence. Yet in Virginia, if I have not been misinformed, elections under the former government were septennial. I bring up this example not as proof of any special merit, since the priority in those instances was probably accidental. Still less do I offer it as proof of any advantage in SEPTENNIAL elections, which are unacceptable when compared with more frequent ones. I offer it merely as proof, and I think a very substantial proof, that the liberties of the people can be in no danger from BIENNIAL elections.

Three further circumstances considerably strengthen the conclusion these examples lead to. The first is that the federal legislature will hold only a part of the supreme legislative authority that is vested entirely in the British Parliament, and that the colonial assemblies and the Irish legislature, with a few exceptions, exercised. It is a received and well-founded maxim that, other things being equal, the greater the power, the shorter its duration ought to be; and conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely its duration may be extended. In the second place, it has been shown elsewhere that the federal legislature will be restrained by its dependence on its people, as other legislative bodies are, and will also be watched and controlled by the collateral legislatures of the individual States, which other legislative bodies are not. And in the third place, there is no comparison between the means the more permanent branches of the federal government will have to seduce the House of Representatives from its duty to the people, if they were disposed to try, and the means of influence over the popular branch that the other branches of the governments I have cited possessed. With less power to abuse, therefore, the federal representatives can be less tempted on one side, and will be doubly watched on the other.
